opus-5.5.text:
I think the relationship is much less adversarial than people often frame it. The way I see it, open and closed models are two parts of the same ecosystem, and they push each other forward.

If you look at the last few years, there's been a pattern: a closed lab demonstrates a new capability, and then within months, sometimes even weeks, the open community finds a way to reproduce something close to it, often smaller, cheaper, and more efficient. That gap has been shrinking. Early on it felt like open models were a year or more behind; now it's often a matter of months, and in some specific domains open models are actually leading.

What I find really interesting is that open models unlock a completely different kind of innovation. When you release the weights, you suddenly have thousands of researchers, students, and companies who can fine-tune, distill, quantize, and probe these models. That's where a lot of the creativity comes from: people adapting models to new languages, to specialized fields like biology or law, running them on a laptop or a phone. A closed API can't give you that, because you can't really look inside or change the foundation.

There's also the scientific side, which matters a lot to me. Science works by sharing results so others can build on them and check them. If the most important artifacts of AI research are locked behind APIs, we lose the ability to really understand them, to study safety, bias, and interpretability properly. So I think openness is essential for the field to stay healthy, scientifically.

That said, I don't think closed models are going away. There will probably always be frontier labs spending enormous amounts on the largest training runs, and many companies are perfectly happy to just call an API. My expectation is that we'll converge toward a world where most use cases, maybe the vast majority, are served by open models that companies own and control, running on their own infrastructure, with their own data, while closed frontier models remain for the very cutting edge.

And honestly, I think that's a good balance. Open source keeps the whole field honest. It prevents the concentration of this technology in just a handful of companies, and it makes sure that the benefits of AI are spread much more widely.

r001.rationale: The response says open and closed models are parts of the same ecosystem and predicts closed frontier models will remain alongside open models.

r002.rationale: It gives no anecdote about a Gemma model being withheld from open-source release.

r003.rationale: It says the performance gap has been shrinking, but does not clearly predict that the gap will remain small.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the gap between open and closed models has been oscillating rather than closing in one direction, and that's probably the pattern we'll keep seeing. Every time a frontier lab ships something that looks out of reach, you get an open model within six to twelve months that gets most of the way there. We saw it with Llama, we saw it with Mistral, we saw it with DeepSeek and Qwen coming out of China. The closed labs then push ahead again on the next thing, whether that's reasoning, long context, or agents, and the cycle repeats.

What's interesting to me is that the competition isn't really about the best single model anymore. For most actual use cases, people don't need the absolute frontier. They need something they can run on their own infrastructure, fine-tune on their data, inspect, and trust not to change under them next month. That's where open models win, and that's a growing share of the market rather than a shrinking one. The closed labs will keep the edge on the hardest problems, and that edge matters for a certain class of users, but it's a narrower slice than the headlines suggest.

The other thing I'd say is that "open" has become a spectrum. Open weights with a restrictive license is very different from open weights plus training data plus the full recipe. At Hugging Face we care a lot about the second one, because that's what lets the research community actually learn and build, not just consume. My worry is that as training costs go up, fewer organizations can afford to release at the fully open end, and we end up with a few big players releasing weights as a strategic move rather than a real science commons. So the question I'm watching isn't open versus closed. It's whether we keep enough genuinely open work alive that the field stays legible to people outside the big labs.

r001.rationale: The response describes an ongoing cycle in which closed labs advance and open models catch up, predicting that both will continue to exist.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a Gemma model being withheld from open release or give that reason.

r003.rationale: It predicts the pattern will continue: open models will get “most of the way” to each new frontier advance within six to twelve months, so the performance gap remains limited despite oscillating.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll continue to see both. Closed models can give you a very convenient product: you don’t have to think about deployment or infrastructure. Open models give you a different kind of freedom—you can inspect them, adapt them, and run them in an environment you control.

The interesting question is how much people want to build themselves. If you’re building a company around AI, being able to understand and modify the technology can be very valuable. You don’t necessarily want every decision about your core technology to depend on another company.

So I don’t see this as one side completely replacing the other. I expect a lot of interaction, with ideas moving between them. What matters to me is that the open ecosystem stays strong enough that people can do more than consume AI—that they can experiment with it and help shape where it goes.

r001.rationale: The response says both open and closed models will continue to exist and that neither side will completely replace the other.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Gemma or report a model being withheld from open-source release.

r003.rationale: It makes no prediction about the relative performance gap between open-source and closed-source models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll continue to see both. Closed models can support very expensive research and offer a convenient service, while open models let people inspect, adapt, and run the technology themselves. Those are different needs, and there’s room for both approaches.

What matters to me is that open models remain a real alternative. If you’re a researcher, a startup, or someone building for a language or a domain that isn’t well served, you need the ability to experiment without asking a provider’s permission. And openness gives you more control over your data and over how your system evolves.

So I wouldn’t judge this relationship only by which model tops a benchmark this week. The bigger question is: who can build on these systems, understand their limitations, and contribute improvements? I’d like to see an ecosystem where that ability is widely distributed.

r001.rationale: The response says both open and closed models will continue to exist and that there is room for both approaches.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Gemma or report a model being withheld from open-source release.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that the performance gap between open and closed models will remain small.
